description: Our team brings together undergraduate and graduate students from the Department of Astronautical Engineering,  Physics, Engineering Physics, and  Electrical and Electronics Engineering. Combining diverse academic perspectives, we tackle space challenges creatively. NESY bridges science and engineering to build practical solutions. It is our platform to grow together, collaborate closely, and contribute meaningfully to the future of space exploration
summary:
How can we prepare for living and working on the Moon when we cannot test every challenge directly on its surface?

As Team NESY, we developed an interactive, data-driven platform using NASAEarth observation data and lunar measurements to identify terrestrial environments relevant to Artemis mission preparation. We explore which places on Earth share meaningful characteristics with lunar regions and how these similarities could support astronaut protection, habitat testing, and surface operations.

We focused on three lunar locations: "Marius Hills Pit", with its volcanic terrain and potential subsurface shelters; "Malapert Massif", known for elevated terrain and harsh polar conditions; and "Shackleton Connecting Ridge", relevant to south polar exploration.

Our platform combines three tools: "Analog Suite" evaluates five terrestrial regions—Beishan–Gobi, Tibet–Qaidam, Harrat Khaybar, Central and Eastern Anatolia, and the Andean Altiplano. "Discovery" searches a broader geographical area, while "Top" highlights strong matches in specific environmental domains.

Through environmental screening, similarity analysis, and scientific interpretation, NESY identifies promising Earth analogs while acknowledging the physical limitations of Earth–Moon comparisons.

Our goal is not to find a perfect copy of the Moon on Earth, but to discover where specific lunar challenges can be investigated before future missions.

What It Does & How It Works

We developed NESY to identify terrestrial environments that could support specific lunar research and mission preparation activities through measurable environmental similarities.

Our "Analog Suite" uses Google Earth Engine to process satellite observations from five selected terrestrial regions in 5 × 5 km grid cells. We initially evaluated 9,808 cells and retained 9,326 after environmental and data-quality screening. We then compared 8 indicators covering topography, thermal behavior, spectral characteristics, surface brightness, and moisture against three lunar reference profiles. Our model combines normalized Euclidean similarity (60%) and cosine similarity (40%) to rank potential analog candidates.

To search beyond these predefined regions, we developed "Discovery", which surveyed approximately 1.75 million geographical grid locations and retained 870,889 candidates after screening.

We also developed "Top" to evaluate candidates within four individual domains: Topography & Trafficability, Thermal Regime, Mineralogy & ISRU, and Volatiles & Ice Proxy. Rather than relying on a single overall score, users can investigate which locations match the characteristics most relevant to their research objective.

Our Streamlit interface brings these analyses together through interactive maps, candidate rankings, and Earth–Moon parameter comparisons.

Benefits & Intended Impact

We wanted to address a fundamental challenge in lunar mission preparation: no environment on Earth can reproduce every condition found on the Moon. A location that is suitable for testing rover mobility, for example, may not be equally useful for investigating geological materials or thermal protection.

Our overall analysis identified a Beishan–Gobi candidate for "Shackleton Connecting Ridge" scoring 58.7/100, another Beishan–Gobi candidate for "Malapert Massif" scoring 63.8/100, and a basaltic location in Harrat Khaybar for "Marius Hills Pit" scoring 66.5/100.

However, when we examined individual environmental domains, we found much stronger numerical matches for certain characteristics. Some topographical and mineralogical proxy scores reached approximately 98/100, while thermal similarities remained considerably lower.

This difference is important to our approach. Instead of looking for one location that matches every lunar condition, we can identify different terrestrial environments according to the parameter or engineering challenge being investigated. A strong terrain match may guide preliminary rover mobility research, while a relevant geological match may support material-related studies.

These scores represent relative computational similarity within the selected model and domain, not physical equivalence or confirmed operational suitability.

Our intended impact is to help researchers prioritize promising Earth-based testing environments, making early-stage planning for astronaut protection, habitat development, and lunar surface operations more systematic and accessible.

Tools, Languages & Datasets Used

We used JavaScript in Google Earth Engine for satellite data extraction and geospatial processing. Our environmental filtering, numerical analysis, and similarity-ranking workflows were developed in Python using Pandas and NumPy. We built the interactive platform with Streamlit and used Plotly for data visualization, with GitHub supporting version control and documentation.

For Earth observations, we integrated NASADEM, MODIS Terra, Landsat 9, NASA SMAP, and ESA WorldCover.

For lunar analysis, we used LROC QuickMap terrain and Diviner thermal products, Lunar Prospector compositional and hydrogen-related measurements, Chandrayaan-1 Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M³) spectral data, and the LROC Pits Atlas for Marius Hills Pit morphology.

Creativity & Key Engineering Factors Considered

What makes our approach distinctive is that we do not treat a high overall similarity score as the only measure of a useful lunar analog. We wanted to understand which characteristics could be meaningfully investigated on Earth and which physical differences would require additional engineering consideration.

1. False-Analog Screening

We developed environmental filters targeting vegetation, salt flats, selected loose-sand environments, and moisture-related conditions that could produce misleading similarity scores. Additional water-related checks revealed that some unsuitable candidates still passed the initial screening, helping us identify where further verification is necessary.

2. Mission-Specific Analog Selection

Our "Top" module reflects one of the central ideas behind NESY: different lunar challenges may require different terrestrial analogs.

By examining four environmental domains independently, we can identify locations with strong matches in selected parameters, even when their overall similarity is moderate. This approach helps connect candidate selection to specific research objectives rather than forcing every environmental characteristic into a single recommendation.

The much higher scores observed in some individual domains also demonstrated why domain-specific matching can be informative, provided that these results are interpreted within their scientific limitations.

3. Physics-Based Engineering Interpretation

Even when terrestrial and lunar environments share measurable characteristics, important differences remain in gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation exposure, thermal behavior, and regolith properties.

We therefore examined preliminary engineering relationships involving reduced-gravity bearing capacity, atmospheric convection versus lunar vacuum, simplified radiation attenuation, and regolith-related behavior.

These assessments help identify which physical factors would need to be considered when transferring terrestrial research to lunar applications. They are assumption-dependent engineering estimates rather than experimentally validated design specifications.

Future Development

We aim to improve NESY through higher-resolution datasets, more consistent Earth–Moon parameter comparisons, stronger environmental screening, and more scientifically reliable domain-specific rankings.

We also hope to explore AI-assisted anomaly detection, provide more customizable research tools, and eventually extend our approach to Mars analog environments.

Our longer-term vision is an open-source platform that helps researchers evaluate analog locations according to clearly defined scientific and operational objectives.
